A.6 Nonlinear core correction

Within the pseudopotential approach, the electronic charge density is divided into core and valence contributions. A common way to include the core effects in the Kohn-Sham equations is the nonlinear core correction scheme of Ref. 43. In practice, one determines the charge density of the core electrons nc​(𝐫)n_{\rm c}({\bf r}) only once, before the KS self-consistent cycle, as nc​(𝐫)n_{\rm c}({\bf r}) only depends on the pseudopotentials. The KS equations are still solved only for the valence bands and n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) defined in Eq. 16 remains the valence charge. On the contrary, in Eq. 15 one substitutes EI​[n]E_{\rm I}[n] with EI​[nt]E_{\rm I}[n_{\rm t}] where nt​(𝐫)=n⁡(𝐫)+nc​(𝐫)n_{\rm t}({\bf r})=n({\bf r})+n_{\rm c}({\bf r}) is the total charge density.

By using this approach the third order equations need to be modified. First, in the last term in the right hand side of Eq. 25, one has to replace the three ∂n/∂u𝐪\partial n/\partial u_{\bf q} with the corresponding ∂nt/∂u𝐪\partial n_{\rm t}/\partial u_{\bf q}. Second, one has to include in the r.h.s. of Eq. 25 the two additional terms

∫δ​EI​[nt]δ​n​(𝐫)​∂3nc​(𝐫)∂u𝐪​∂u𝐪′​∂u𝐪′′​𝐝𝐫+3∫δ2​EI​[nt]δ​n​(𝐫)​δ​n​(𝐫′)∂2nc​(𝐫)∂u𝐪​∂u𝐪′∂2nt​(𝐫′)∂u𝐪′′d𝐫d𝐫′\begin{split}{}&\int\frac{\delta E_{\rm I}[n_{\rm t}]}{\delta n({\bf r})}\frac{\partial^{3}n_{\rm c}({\bf r})}{\partial u_{{\bf q}}\partial u_{{\bf q}^{\prime}}\partial u_{{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}}}d{\bf r}\\ {}&+3\int\frac{\delta^{2}E_{\rm I}[n_{\rm t}]}{\delta n({\bf r})\delta n({\bf r^{\prime}})}\frac{\partial^{2}n_{\rm c}({\bf r})}{\partial u_{{\bf q}}\partial u_{{\bf q}^{\prime}}}\frac{\partial^{2}n_{\rm t}({\bf r^{\prime}})}{\partial u_{{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}}}d{\bf r}d{\bf r^{\prime}}\end{split} (39)

Appendix B Notes on the implementation

This section discusses some practical issues concerning the actual implementation of the method.

B.1 Implementation

Let us consider three wavevectors in the general case in which 𝐪≠𝐪′≠𝐪′′{\bf q}\neq{\bf q}^{\prime}\neq{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}, with 𝐪+𝐪′+𝐪′′=𝟎{\bf q}+{\bf q}^{\prime}+{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}={\bf 0}. The calculations of the third order derivatives is done in three consecutive steps.

  1. 1.

    Self consistent calculation to obtain the ground state charge n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) and the Kohn-Sham potential VKS​(𝐫)V^{\rm KS}({\bf r}).

  2. 2.

    Self consistent linear response calculation to determine ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪~\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\tilde{\bf q}} and ∂VKS​(𝐫)/∂u𝐪~\partial V^{\rm KS}({\bf r})/\partial u_{\tilde{\bf q}}. This is done three times for the three cases 𝐪~=𝐪′\tilde{\bf q}={\bf q}^{\prime}, 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}, and 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}.

  3. 3.

    Calculation of the third order derivatives.

In order to do Step 3, seven distinct sets of ground-state wavefunctions |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle are needed (see eq. 26 or 27): |ψ𝐤⟩|\psi_{\bf k}\rangle, |ψ𝐤+𝐪~⟩|\psi_{\bf k+\tilde{q}}\rangle, |ψ𝐤−𝐪~⟩|\psi_{\bf k-\tilde{q}}\rangle, with 𝐪~\tilde{\bf q}=q, 𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime}, and 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}, where k runs on the ensemble of wavevectors which are used in the electronic integration. The |ψ𝐤⟩|\psi_{\bf k}\rangle are already calculated in Step 1. They can be saved and read from disk or they can be calculated a second time with a relatively inexpensive non self-consistent solution of the KS equation (based on the knowledge of V𝐊𝐒V^{\bf KS} and n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) determined in Step 1). When k runs on a regular grid and 𝐪~\tilde{\bf q} belongs to the grid, the different sets might coincide. However, given the way the code is implemented  [15] (the wavefunctions are read and written from sequential files; different processors might work with different k points in parallel) it is bests to keep distinct the seven sets.

Twelve distinct sets of wavefunctions derivatives are also needed: |ϕ𝐤q~⟩|\phi^{\tilde{q}}_{\bf k}\rangle, |ϕ𝐤−q~⟩|\phi^{-\tilde{q}}_{\bf k}\rangle, |ϕ𝐤−𝐪~q~⟩|\phi^{\tilde{q}}_{\bf k-\tilde{q}}\rangle, and |ϕ𝐤+𝐪~−q~⟩|\phi^{-\tilde{q}}_{\bf k+\tilde{q}}\rangle, with 𝐪~\tilde{\bf q}=q, 𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime}, and 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}. These wavefunctions can be calculated with a non self-consistent solution of the linearized KS equation which is based on the knowledge of the ∂VKS​(𝐫)/∂u𝐪~\partial V^{\rm KS}({\bf r})/\partial u_{\tilde{\bf q}} calculated in Step 2. Even in this case, for practical reasons, it is better to keep distinct the twelve sets even when some of them coincide. These derivatives are computed resolving non-self-consistently eq. 14; in the present work, this was the most CPU intensive step; on the other hand, for bigger systems the Input/Output of ∂n/∂u𝐪\partial n/\partial u_{\bf q} can become a bottleneck.

In order to evaluate Eq. 26, one needs to calculate matrix elements of the kind ⟨ϕ𝐤−𝐪|V𝐪′|ϕ𝐤𝐪′′⟩\langle\phi^{\bf-q}_{\bf k}|V^{{\bf q}^{\prime}}|\phi^{{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}}_{\bf k}\rangle and ⟨ψ𝐤−𝐪′|V𝐪′′|ψ𝐤+𝐪⟩\langle\psi_{\bf k-q^{\prime}}|V^{{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}}|\psi_{\bf k+q}\rangle. In both cases this calculation has to be done six times for all the possible permutations of the three wavevectors 𝐪{\bf q}, 𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime}, 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}. For the metallic case, Eq. 27, further terms are needed. The terms ⟨ϕ𝐤+𝐪a−𝐪a|V𝐪b|ψ𝐤+𝐪b⟩\langle\phi^{{\bf-q}_{a}}_{{\bf k+q}_{a}}|V^{{\bf q}_{b}}|\psi_{{\bf k}+{\bf q}_{b}}\rangle need to be computed six times for 𝐪a{\bf q}_{a} and 𝐪b{\bf q}_{b} equal to 𝐪{\bf q},𝐪′{\bf q^{\prime}}, 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}, with 𝐪a≠𝐪b{\bf q}_{a}\neq{\bf q}_{b}. The terms ⟨ψ𝐤+𝐪|V𝐪|ψ𝐤⟩\langle\psi_{\bf k+q}|V^{{\bf q}}|\psi_{\bf k}\rangle and ⟨ψ𝐤−𝐪|V−𝐪|ψ𝐤⟩\langle\psi_{\bf k-q}|V^{{\bf-q}}|\psi_{\bf k}\rangle are computed already in Step 2 and can be saved for later use in Step 3. The terms ⟨ψ𝐤−𝐪|V𝐪′|ψ𝐤+𝐪′′⟩\langle\psi_{\bf k-q}|V^{{\bf q^{\prime}}}|\psi_{\bf k+q^{\prime\prime}}\rangle need to be computed for the six permutations of 𝐪{\bf q}, 𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime}, and 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}.

In some special cases the number of operations can be greatly reduced. The most obvious one is when 𝐪=𝐪′=𝐪′′=𝟎{\bf q}={\bf q}^{\prime}={\bf q}^{\prime\prime}={\bf 0}: in this case only one set of wavefunctions derivatives is needed: |ϕ𝐤𝟎⟩|\phi^{\bf 0}_{\bf k}\rangle. Moreover, when 𝐪=𝟎{\bf q}={\bf 0}, 𝐪′=−𝐪′′=𝐩{\bf q}^{\prime}=-{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}={\bf p}, with 𝐩≠𝟎{\bf p}\neq{\bf 0}, only three sets of wavefunctions derivatives are needed: |ϕ𝐤𝟎⟩|\phi^{\bf 0}_{\bf k}\rangle, |ϕ𝐤𝐪⟩|\phi^{\bf q}_{\bf k}\rangle, and |ϕ𝐤−𝐪𝐪⟩|\phi^{\bf q}_{\bf k-q}\rangle. This is because ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u−𝐪=[∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪]∗\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf-q}=[\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q}]^{*} and, according to time reversal symmetry, ϕ−𝐤−𝐪​(𝐫)=[ϕ𝐤𝐪​(𝐫)]∗\phi^{\bf-q}_{\bf-k}({\bf r})=[\phi^{\bf q}_{\bf k}({\bf r})]^{*}. Another special case is when 𝐪=2​𝐩{\bf q}=2{\bf p}, 𝐪′=𝐪′′=−𝐩{\bf q}^{\prime}={\bf q}^{\prime\prime}=-{\bf p}; in this case 8 derivatives are needed and index permutation can be used to avoid computing some terms.

B.2 Symmetry and q-points

A Bravais lattice can be invariant under a certain number, up to 48, of rotations. A crystal will respect a subset, possibly all, of these symmetries defining the group of crystal symmetries, 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. These symmetries can be exploited to reduce the computational cost of the calculation and must be enforced to avoid unphysical breaking of symmetry caused by computational noise. Here, we briefly revise how this is done in the pwscf and phonon codes of Quantum ESPRESSO, and we describe how the approach has been extended to the third order.

In the ground-state energy calculation, the Kohn-Sham equations (Eqs.  14,  15,  16), are not solved for all the k-points of the chosen grid. Instead they are solved only for a subset of k-points which are inequivalent under the rotations of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} (these k points belong to the so called irreducible wedge of the Brillouin zone). The charge density n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) is then obtained, inexpensively, by summing on this k-point subset and, then, by imposing the symmetries of the crystal. The symmetries are imposed by rotating the initial charge density according to all the symmetries and, then, by making the average. In general, even if the crystal has no symmetries, the sum can be performed on half of the k-points of the initial grid since ψ−𝐤​(𝐫)=ψ𝐤∗​(𝐫)\psi_{\bf-k}({\bf r})=\psi^{*}_{\bf k}({\bf r}) (time reversal symmetry).

In the phonon calculation, the situation depends on the phonon wave-vector q. Let us consider the the symmetries of the crystal which are associated with a rotation that leaves q unchanged (or that transform 𝐪{\bf q} into an equivalent 𝐪+𝐆{\bf q+G}). This subgroup of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is called the small group of q, 𝒢𝐪{\mathcal{G}}_{\bf q}. The linear response equations (Eqs.  20,  21,  22) are not solved on the grid. Instead, they are solved only for a subset of k-points which are inequivalent under the rotations of 𝒢𝐪{\mathcal{G}}_{\bf q}. ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} is obtained by summing on this k-point subset and, then, by imposing the symmetries of 𝒢𝐪{\mathcal{G}}_{\bf q} (in analogy with n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) in the previous paragraph). Because of time reversal symmetry, in order to obtain ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} from Eq. 22 one needs to compute explicitly only the |ϕ𝐤𝐪⟩|\phi^{\bf q}_{\bf k}\rangle but not the |ϕ𝐤−𝐪⟩|\phi^{\bf-q}_{\bf k}\rangle. However, if there are no other symmetries, the sum has to be performed on all the k-points of the grid and not on half as in the total energy calculation. Once that ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} has been calculated, one can determine the dynamical matrix at q.

Another way in which the symmetries can be exploited is the following. The ensemble of the vectors obtained by rotating q with all the rotations of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is called the star of q. The number of inequivalent vectors in the star is |𝒢|/|𝒢𝐪||{\mathcal{G}}|/|{\mathcal{G}}_{\bf q}|, where |𝒢||{\mathcal{G}}| is the order of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. Once that ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} has been determined, all the ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪~\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\tilde{\bf q}} for the vectors 𝐪~\tilde{\bf q} in the star can be obtained inexpensively by rotation. Moreover, because of time reversal symmetry ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u−𝐪=[∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪]∗\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{-{\bf q}}=[\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{{\bf q}}]^{*}.

A third-order calculation is conceptually not different. In this case we are dealing with a triplet of points (q,q′,q′′)({\textbf{q}},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime\prime}) and one has to consider the small group of the rotations of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} that leave the three q-points unchanged, 𝒢𝐪,𝐪′,𝐪′′{\mathcal{G}}_{{\bf q,q^{\prime},q^{\prime\prime}}}. The electronic k-point summation in Eq. 26,  27 (and also those in Eqs. 37,  38) is done on a subset of point of the initial grid which are inequivalent under the rotations of 𝒢𝐪,𝐪′,𝐪′′{\mathcal{G}}_{{\bf q,q^{\prime},q^{\prime\prime}}}. The third order matrix obtained from this partial summation is not useful as it is. The actual third order matrix is obtained by imposing on it the symmetries of 𝒢𝐪,𝐪′,𝐪′′{\mathcal{G}}_{{\bf q,q^{\prime},q^{\prime\prime}}}.

In analogy to the dynamical matrix case, once the third-order matrix of a given (q,q′,q′′)({\textbf{q}},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime\prime}) triplet has been determined, on can apply the rotations ℛ{\mathcal{R}} of the crystal symmetry group 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} and obtain inexpensively the matrices corresponding to the rotated triplet (ℛ​𝐪,ℛ​𝐪′,ℛ​𝐪′′)({\mathcal{R}}{\bf q},{\mathcal{R}}{\bf q^{\prime}},{\mathcal{R}}{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}). Moreover, the matrix of the triplet (−q,−q′,−q′′)(-{\textbf{q}},-{\textbf{q}}^{\prime},-{\textbf{q}}^{\prime\prime}) can be obtained by conjugation. Another useful symmetry is the trivial one associated to the index permutation: by construction, the matrix associated with the triplet (q,q′,q′′)({\textbf{q}},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime},{\textbf{q}}^{\prime\prime}) is equal to the six matrices obtained by permuting the three vectors 𝐪{\bf q},𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime},𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime} and the corresponding indices.

B.3 Discretisation on a grid

In some cases, it is useful to calculate the third-order matrices on a regular grid of q wavevectors in the Brillouin zone, the reason for this are clarified in Sec. C. When we say that calculations are done on a given grid, it means that we have calculated the third order coefficients corresponding to every triplet (𝐪,𝐪′,𝐪′′)({\bf q},{\bf q}^{\prime},{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}) of points, such that each vector belongs to the grid and that the condition 𝐪+𝐪′+𝐪′′=G{\bf q}+{\bf q}^{\prime}+{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}=G is satisfied.

In the actual implementation of the procedure, we first determine ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} and the dynamical matrices on the grid of q wavevector. Exploiting the symmetries can allow an important reduction of the computational cost. Indeed, the actual ab-initio calculation is done only for those q points which do not belong to the same star (defined in the previous section), or which are not equivalent to the opposite of a point already calculated. ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} and the dynamical matrices for the other points are then obtained by rotation or conjugation. Once this is done we perform the third order calculations.

In practice, we can perform a double loop on the grid and chose 𝐪{\bf q} and 𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime} so that they belong to the grid. The third vector is chosen as 𝐪′′=−𝐪−𝐪′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime}=-{\bf q}-{\bf q}^{\prime}. 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime} may not belong to the grid. 𝐪′′{\bf q}^{\prime\prime} is however still connected to a point in grid by a reciprocal lattice vector G and, thanks to Eq.  29, we are not losing generality. Moreover,

∂n⁡(𝐫)∂u𝐪′′=∂n⁡(𝐫)∂u𝐪′′+𝐆\frac{\partial n({\bf r})}{\partial u_{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}}=\frac{\partial n({\bf r})}{\partial u_{\bf q^{\prime\prime}+G}}

for every reciprocal space vector G, and we can use the ∂n⁡(𝐫)/∂u𝐪\partial n({\bf r})/\partial u_{\bf q} calculated on the original grid. Once that a triplet has been computed we can determine for free all the triplets which are equivalent by rotation, permutation of the indices, or by conjugation. Actually, some of these operations can be redundant, e.g. a certain rotation could be equivalent to a permutation, or to a conjugation. The triplet obtained in this way are deleted from the list of the “triplets to be done” and will not be computed in the following step of the loop. This procedure allows for a spectacular reduction in the number of triplets; in the graphene case 4096 possible triplets are reduced to just 88 independent triplets.

Appendix C Fourier interpolation

Actual DFPT calculations are done on a relatively coarse grid of q wavevectors. Dynamical matrices and third order coefficients are then obtained for a finer grid with a Fourier interpolation technique. In this section, first, we revise the Fourier interpolation technique as it is implemented in the standard Quantum ESPRESSO package. Then, we describe how the method has been generalized to third order force constants.

C.1 Second order

Let us consider a lattice with basis 𝐚1{\bf a}_{1}, 𝐚2{\bf a}_{2}, 𝐚3{\bf a}_{3}. The dynamical matrices D2​(𝐪ss′)D_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf q}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right) (we use the definition of Eq. 2 and we drop for simplicity the Cartesian indexes) are first computed ab initio on a uniform grid, centered in the origin, of N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} q points of the Brillouin zone. We want to determine the real space force constants

F2​(𝐑ss′)=∂2ℰtot∂v𝟎,s​∂v𝐑,s′F_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\frac{\partial^{2}{\cal E}^{\rm tot}}{\partial v_{{\bf 0},s}\partial v_{{\bf R},s^{\prime}}} (40)

by Fourier interpolation of the D2D_{2} from the N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} grid. D2D_{2} for a generic q point can then be obtained by back Fourier interpolation.

Let us consider

F~2(𝐑ss′)=1Nt∑𝐪D2(𝐪ss′)e−i𝐪⋅𝐑,\tilde{F}_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\frac{1}{N_{\rm t}}\sum_{\bf q}D_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf q}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}}, (41)

where R is a lattice vector, Nt=N1​N2​N3N_{\rm t}=N_{1}N_{2}N_{3}, and the sum is performed on the points of the grid. The F~2\tilde{F}_{2} defined in this way cannot be used as they are since they are unphysical long-ranged constants. Indeed, F~2​(𝐑+𝐑¯ss′)=F~2​(𝐑ss′)\tilde{F}_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}+\overline{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\tilde{F}_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right) for any 𝐑¯\overline{\bf R} vector of the super lattice (SL) generated by the lattice vectors 𝐀1=N1​𝐚1{\bf A}_{1}=N_{1}{\bf a}_{1}, 𝐀2=N2​𝐚2{\bf A}_{2}=N_{2}{\bf a}_{2}, 𝐀3=N3​𝐚2{\bf A}_{3}=N_{3}{\bf a}_{2}.

The short-ranged F2F_{2} can be obtained from the F~2\tilde{F}_{2} in the following way. We define two vectors as “SL equivalent” when their difference is a vector of the super lattice defined by 𝐀1{\bf A}_{1}, 𝐀2{\bf A}_{2}, 𝐀3{\bf A}_{3} and we call WSLW_{\rm SL} as the Wigner-Seitz of this super lattice. Eq. 40 is the force constant between the atoms whose distance is 𝐝=𝐑+𝐭s′−𝐭s{\bf d}={\bf R}+{\bf t}_{s^{\prime}}-{\bf t}_{s}, where 𝐭s{\bf t}_{s} is the position of the atom ss in the unit cell. We distinguish three cases: i) when 𝐝∈WSL{\bf d}\in W_{\rm SL}, F2​(𝐑ss′)=F~2​(𝐑ss′)F_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\tilde{F}_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right); ii) when d lies on the border of WSLW_{\rm SL}, F2​(𝐑ss′)=F~2​(𝐑ss′)/NeqF_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\tilde{F}_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)/N_{\rm eq}, where NeqN_{\rm eq} is the number of points on the border of WSLW_{\rm SL} which are “SL equivalent” to d; iii) when 𝐝∉WSL{\bf d}\notin W_{\rm SL}, F2​(𝐑ss′)=0F_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=0. The interpolated dynamical matrix for a generic q is then

D2​(𝐪ss′)=∑𝐑F2​(𝐑ss′)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑,D_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf q}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\sum_{\bf R}F_{2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}&{\bf R}\\ s&s^{\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}}, (42)

where the sum is done on all the lattice vectors R. This is the Fourier interpolation technique as it is implemented in the standard Quantum ESPRESSO package.

C.2 Third order

For the third order coefficients the situation is analogous, although less straightforward. We use the notation:

D3​(𝐪𝐪′𝐪′′ss′s′′)=1N​∂3ℰtot∂u𝐪,s​∂u𝐪′,s′​∂u𝐪′′,s′′,F3​(𝐑𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)=∂3ℰtot∂v𝐑,s​∂v𝐑′,s′​∂v𝐑′′,s′′.\begin{split}D_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf q}&{\bf q^{\prime}}&{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)={}&\frac{1}{N}\frac{\partial^{3}{\cal E}^{\rm tot}}{\partial u_{{\bf q},s}\partial u_{{\bf q^{\prime}},s^{\prime}}\partial u_{{\bf q^{\prime\prime}},s^{\prime\prime}}},\\ F_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf R}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)={}&\frac{\partial^{3}{\cal E}^{\rm tot}}{\partial v_{{\bf R},s}\partial v_{{\bf R^{\prime}},s^{\prime}}\partial v_{{\bf R^{\prime\prime}},s^{\prime\prime}}}.\end{split} (43)

The matrices D3D_{3} are first computed ab initio on a uniform grid of q points centered in the origin, meaning that both vectors q′ and q′′ run on the grid, while 𝐪=−𝐪′−𝐪′′{\bf q}=-{\bf q^{\prime}}-{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}. We then define

F~3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)=1Nt2​∑𝐪′,𝐪′′D3​(𝐪𝐪′𝐪′′ss′s′′)​e−i⁡(𝐪′⋅𝐑′+𝐪′′⋅𝐑′′),\tilde{F}_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\frac{1}{N_{\rm t}^{2}}\sum_{{\bf q^{\prime}},{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}}D_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf q}&{\bf q^{\prime}}&{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)e^{-i({\bf q^{\prime}}\cdot{\bf R^{\prime}}+{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}\cdot{\bf R^{\prime\prime}})}, (44)

where the sums are performed on the grid points.

The force constants F3F_{3} of Eq. 43 correspond to three atoms at the positions 𝐭s{\bf t}_{s}, 𝐭s′+𝐑′{\bf t}_{s^{\prime}}+{\bf R^{\prime}}, and 𝐭s′′+𝐑′′{\bf t}_{s^{\prime\prime}}+{\bf R^{\prime\prime}} (because of the crystal translational symmetry we can consider without loss of generality R=0). The three atoms form a triangle with perimeter P=|𝐝1|+|𝐝2|+|𝐝3|P=|{\bf d}_{1}|+|{\bf d}_{2}|+|{\bf d}_{3}|, where 𝐝1{\bf d}_{1}, 𝐝2{\bf d}_{2}, 𝐝3{\bf d}_{3} are the distances among the three atoms (the three sides of the triangle). To determine F3F_{3} we consider three cases. i) When all the three distances 𝐝1,𝐝2,𝐝3{\bf d}_{1},{\bf d}_{2},{\bf d}_{3} are inside (and not on the border) of WSLW_{\rm SL}, we put F3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)=F~3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)F_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\tilde{F}_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right). ii) If two of the distances (e.g. 𝐝1,𝐝2{\bf d}_{1},{\bf d}_{2}) are inside WSLW_{\rm SL} and the third one is outside or on the border of WSLW_{\rm SL} we calculate the perimeter PP of the triangle. If PP is the shortest perimeter among the perimeters of all the triangles formed by the triplet of atoms “SL equivalent” to the original three, we put F3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)=F~3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)/NeqF_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\tilde{F}_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)/N_{\rm eq}, where NeqN_{\rm eq} is the number of triangles with perimeter equal to PP. iii) In all the other cases F3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)=0F_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=0.

The interpolated D3D_{3} matrices for a generic triplet of wavevectors (such that 𝐪+𝐪′+𝐪′′=𝐆{\bf q}+{\bf q^{\prime}}+{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}={\bf G}) is obtained from

D3​(𝐪𝐪′𝐪′′ss′s′′)=∑𝐑′,𝐑′′F3​(𝟎𝐑′𝐑′′ss′s′′)​ei⁡(𝐪′⋅𝐑′+𝐪′′⋅𝐑′′),D_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf q}&{\bf q^{\prime}}&{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\sum_{{\bf R^{\prime}},{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}}F_{3}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}{\bf 0}&{\bf R^{\prime}}&{\bf R^{\prime\prime}}\\ s&s^{\prime}&s^{\prime\prime}\end{smallmatrix}\right)e^{i({\bf q^{\prime}}\cdot{\bf R^{\prime}}+{\bf q^{\prime\prime}}\cdot{\bf R^{\prime\prime}})}, (45)

where the sums run on all the lattice vectors. The criterion presently described to determine the F3F_{3}s, stems from the assumption of a long range exponential decay of the force constants.

Appendix D Computational details

D.1 Electronic integration

The electronic integration of the density functional theory calculations is done using a first-order Methfessel-Paxton smearing[39] of 0.020.02 Ry which converges for a grid of 32×32×132\times 32\times 1 electronic k-points in simple and bilayer graphene and for a grid of 32×32×832\times 32\times 8 k-points for graphite.

D.2 Linear response calculations

DFT dynamical matrices are corrected using a procedure based on DFT+GW renormalization of the electron-phonon interaction as in Ref. 31. Indeed, DFT reproduces very well the measured dispersions of graphite for all the phonon branches but for the TO one, in the vicinity of the high symmetry point K. This failure of DFT, which is very specific to the graphene and graphite systems, has been analyzed in Ref. 31. To improve the accuracy of the TO phonon branch, we have applied an electron-phonon self-interaction as described in Ref. 31. The detailed procedure is described in Sec. IIB of Ref. 44 (third paragraph). We have used the parameter rG​W=1.65r^{GW}=1.65, which is appropriate to the present LDA calculations and which can be derived from Table I of Ref. 31. Using this approach we determined the dynamical matrices of graphene on a super-sampled 48×48×148\times 48\times 1 q-point grid. The matrices for the graphite and for the bilayer are then obtained by using as in-plane force constants those of graphene and as out-of-plane force constants those coming from independent DFPT calculations on the two systems.

The third order coefficients are obtained in the standard way, that is without including this self-interaction correction of Ref. 31. For graphene, the third-order coefficients are calculated on a 8×8×18\times 8\times 1 q-point grid (see Sec. B.3), which consists in 88 irreducible triplets. For bulk graphite, third-order coefficients are calculated on a 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 grid, which consists in 297 irreducible q triplets. When computing the linewidth, we have tested convergence starting from the 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 grid coefficients, finding that the use of the those from the 4×4×24\times 4\times 2 subset grid (33 inequivalent triplets) does not worsen accuracy. For bilayer graphene, the third-order coefficients are calculated on a 4×4×14\times 4\times 1 q-point grid (12 irreducible triplets).

D.3 Broadening calculations

Eqs. 6 and 7 are evaluated by performing the sum over a discrete uniform grid of 𝐪{\bf q} points randomly shifted from the origin. The δ⁡(x)\delta(x) distribution is substituted with the Gaussian function δ~​(x)=e−(x/χ)2/(χ​π)\tilde{\delta}(x)=e^{-(x/\chi)^{2}}/(\chi\sqrt{\pi}), where χ\chi is an artificial smearing, independent from q. The results of Sects. III.1 and  III.2 are obtained by using: for graphene, a 1800×1800×11800\times 1800\times 1 grid and χ=1\chi=1 cm-1; for graphite, 600×600×15600\times 600\times 15 grid and χ=5\chi=5 cm-1; for the bilayer, a 1200×1200×11200\times 1200\times 1 grid and χ=2\chi=2 cm-1. The results of Sec. III.3 are obtained using: for graphene, a 128×128×1128\times 128\times 1 grid and χ=10\chi=10 cm-1; for graphite and bilayer, a 64×64×464\times 64\times 4 grid and χ=10\chi=10 cm-1. For each system, the same grid is used to determine the broadening from Eq. 6 and the thermal conductivity from Eq. 7. The convergence, has been tested using smaller smearing values and finer grids at selected temperatures.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
